points.description: States that the energy of light is proportional to its frequency (E ∝ f, or E = hf); accept equivalent wording such as higher-frequency light has higher energy, provided the proportional relationship is clear.
points.partial_credit: Part marks for saying higher frequency means more energy without stating proportionality.

levels.says: Says higher-frequency light has more energy, but does not state that energy is proportional to frequency or give E = hf.

points.description: States that the energy levels of an electron in an atom are quantized (discrete, not continuous).

Explains that for excitation, the absorbed light energy (or frequency) must exactly equal the energy difference between two electron energy levels (E = hf = ΔE); because the level gaps are fixed, only certain frequencies can be absorbed.
points.partial_credit: Part marks for saying the energy must match an energy-level difference without clearly linking this to only certain frequencies being absorbed.

levels.says: States that absorbed light must match an energy-level difference, but does not clearly explain that this allows only specific frequencies to be absorbed.

points.description: States that a minimum energy, or threshold frequency, is needed to eject an electron from the atom.
States that any photon energy above the minimum/threshold energy becomes kinetic energy of the ejected electron (K = E_photon − threshold energy).
points.partial_credit: Part marks for saying extra energy is not lost or is carried away, without identifying it as kinetic energy of the ejected electron.

levels.says: Says extra energy above the threshold is not lost or is carried away, but does not identify it as kinetic energy of the ejected electron.

rubric.notes: Full marks require all five ideas: light energy is proportional to frequency, electron energy levels are quantized, excitation requires an exact energy-level gap, ejection has a minimum threshold, and excess energy becomes kinetic energy. Part marks are available on P1, P3 and P5 for partially correct statements. No marks are earned for answers that say any frequency can excite an electron or that confuse excitation with ejection.
